The photocatalytic activity of iron-based metal-organic frameworks (Fe-MOFs) for CO2 reduction can be significantly enhanced by a synergistic approach that combines the incorporation of polyaniline as a tailored conductive polymer with controlled electrostatic assembly of cationic photosensitizers, such as [Ru(phen)3]2+, into the Fe-MOF structure. This integrated system will not only improve charge transfer efficiency and light absorption through optimized heterojunction formations but also leverage a design of experiments (DoE) approach to systematically refine key parameters (such as pH, ionic strength, and molar ratios) during the assembly process. We anticipate this combination to yield at least a 50% increase in CO2 conversion rates compared to unmodified Fe-MOF systems, with a selectivity for CO production exceeding 90%, and we will utilize UV-Vis spectroscopy and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to provide quantitative metrics for charge transfer efficiency.

The photocatalytic activity of iron-based metal-organic frameworks (Fe-MOFs) for CO2 reduction can be significantly enhanced through the controlled electrostatic assembly of specifically selected cationic photosensitizers, such as [Ru(phen)3]2+, with anionic Fe-MOFs under optimized conditions (pH 7, ionic strength of 0.1 M, and a molar ratio of Fe-MOF to photosensitizer of 20:1). This assembly will improve charge transfer efficiency, leading to at least a 30% increase in CO2 conversion rates when measured by gas chromatography compared to unassembled systems.

The photocatalytic activity of iron-based metal-organic frameworks (Fe-MOFs) for CO2 reduction can be significantly enhanced through the incorporation of UV-responsive polymeric films that encapsulate cationic photosensitizers, such as [Ru(phen)3]2+, utilizing a layer-by-layer deposition technique consisting of five alternating layers of polymer and photosensitizer. Each layer will be deposited under controlled conditions of 25°C and 60% humidity over a 24-hour period to ensure uniformity. Characterization will employ gas chromatography to measure CO2 conversion rates and UV-Vis spectroscopy to monitor charge separation efficiency. This approach aims to facilitate directed charge migration through the polymer matrix, resulting in a predicted enhancement of CO2 conversion rates by at least 40% compared to conventional photocatalytic systems, supported by control experiments with uncoated Fe-MOFs and a series of comparative studies under similar conditions.
